opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was the moment it did something that our own operators initially thought was wrong.

When we first started letting the system make recommendations in Google's data centers, a lot of what it suggested was sensible: small tweaks to setpoints, the kinds of things a really diligent engineer might do if they had time to watch every sensor all day. That was impressive, but it wasn't creative. It was just very good at the job we already understood.

Then there were cases where it would propose a strategy that cut against conventional wisdom. Data center cooling has decades of rules of thumb baked into it: run equipment this way, stage chillers in this order, keep this setpoint here. The system would come back with something like, "Actually, run more equipment at lower load," or it would take advantage of outdoor weather conditions in a way that wasn't in anyone's playbook. The first reaction from the facility team was skepticism, sometimes outright, "That's a bug."

But when we dug into it, the physics checked out. It had found a trade-off in the system that humans hadn't been exploiting, not because people weren't smart, but because the space of possible configurations is enormous and nobody can hold all those interactions in their head at once. Our operators had experience and heuristics. The AI had the ability to explore the whole space and evaluate consequences across thousands of variables.

What made it feel creative wasn't just that it was different. Lots of things are different and wrong. It was that it was different, correct, and then the experts learned from it. Some of those strategies became things the operators started thinking about themselves. It's a bit like what happened with AlphaGo and move 37: a move that looked like a mistake until you understood it, and then it changed how people thought about the game.

For me, that was the turning point. It stopped being an automation tool and started looking like a collaborator, something that could expand what the people running these facilities thought was possible.

r001.rationale: It says operators and experts learned from the AI, but does not state that Jim Gao personally learned something he did not know or that he helped design the system.

r002.rationale: It describes strategies that surprised operators and were later validated, but does not clearly say those decisions saved energy.

r003.rationale: It frames the AI’s novel, correct discoveries as creative, but does not clearly characterize that creativity as discovering knowledge from raw data.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I'll be honest — when we started, I didn't think of it as creative at all. I thought of it as a control problem. We had this enormous data center cooling system at Google, chillers and cooling towers and pumps and all these setpoints, and the hypothesis was really simple: a model that can see thousands of sensors at once should be able to find a lower-energy operating point than a human looking at a handful of dashboards. That's optimization. That's not what I'd call creative.

The moment that changed my mind was when we actually let it drive. We'd been running it in recommendation mode first — the AI suggests, the operators decide. And the operators kept rejecting certain recommendations because they looked wrong. Not dangerous, just wrong. The system would want to run more chillers than seemed necessary, or push a water temperature in a direction that every rule of thumb said was backwards. And the human instinct is, "That's a bug."

Then we got to the point where it could operate autonomously within safety constraints, and we let it do those things. And they worked. And when we went back and reconstructed why, it wasn't anything mystical. It had figured out something like, if you spread the load across more units at partial capacity, the total energy is lower than running fewer units hard, because of how efficiency curves bend. Or that a specific combination of outside air temperature and humidity made a counterintuitive setpoint pay off.

But here's the thing — some of our best engineers had decades in this field, and none of them had done that. Not because they couldn't understand it afterward. They could. It just wasn't in anyone's playbook. The playbook had been written for humans who can hold maybe five variables in their head at once, so it's full of conservative heuristics. The model had no playbook. It just had the data and the objective.

So I came around to thinking that "creative" might be the honest word for it. Because what is creativity, really, if not finding a solution that works, that nobody in the room would have proposed, and that makes everyone go, "Huh, I should have seen that"? It wasn't creative in the sense of having intent or taste. But functionally, from the perspective of the people operating the plant, it was producing ideas, and the ideas were good.

And the deeper lesson for me was less about the AI and more about us. It showed me how much of what we call expertise is actually accumulated caution. We'd confused the limits of our own attention with the limits of the system.

r001.rationale: The response says the model found strategies the engineers had not proposed, but it does not state that it taught Jim Gao something about a system he had helped design.

r002.rationale: It says operators rejected recommendations that looked wrong, then reports that those counterintuitive strategies worked and lowered total energy.

r003.rationale: It describes the model using data and an objective, without a human playbook, to find effective solutions nobody had proposed, and calls that functionally creative.

astra-6.text:
What convinced me was seeing it find strategies that hadn’t occurred to us. In a data center, you have all these interacting pieces of equipment—pumps, cooling towers, chillers—and changing one affects the others. As engineers, we tend to break that complexity into manageable pieces. The AI could look at the whole system and find combinations of settings that seemed counterintuitive but worked better together.

I don’t mean creative in the sense that it had imagination or intent. I mean it found a useful solution outside the set of solutions we were considering. That was the exciting part: it could teach us something about a system we thought we understood.

r001.rationale: It says the AI could teach people something about a system they thought they understood, but does not say Jim had helped design that system.

r002.rationale: It describes counterintuitive settings that worked better, but does not specify energy-saving decisions or clearly identify human operators’ expectations.

r003.rationale: It calls the AI’s unexpected solution-finding exciting and discusses creativity, but does not connect creativity to discovering new knowledge from raw data.

sol-6.1.text:
What convinced me was seeing it come up with operating strategies that hadn’t occurred to us. You give it an objective—reduce energy use while keeping the data center within its operating limits—but you don’t tell it exactly how to get there. And it starts finding different ways to coordinate the cooling equipment.

The interesting moment is when you look at a recommendation and think, “That seems counterintuitive.” Then you work through the physics and realize it makes sense. It’s finding an interaction you hadn’t considered. To me, that’s a practical kind of creativity: discovering a useful solution beyond the ones we thought to give it.

r001.rationale: The response says the AI found strategies and interactions the team had not considered, but does not say it taught Gao about a system he helped design.

r002.rationale: It describes recommendations as counterintuitive, but does not clearly state that successful energy-saving decisions contradicted human operators’ expectations.

r003.rationale: It calls discovering useful solutions a practical kind of creativity, but does not characterize discovering new knowledge from raw data as creativity.
